metadata.file_name: 47. Haw & King. (2023). Understanding Filipino students’ achievement in PISA_ The roles of personal characteristics, proximal processes, and social contexts.pdf
metadata.title: Understanding Filipino students’ achievement in PISA: The roles of personal characteristics, proximal processes, and social contexts

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 Philippine microdata, which includes weights to account for PISA’s complex two-stage sampling (schools first, then students within schools). The authors state that the published dataset includes weights and that they used these weights for classical statistical inferences (correlation/regression) to obtain unbiased estimates. For the hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) step, they additionally use the 80 replicate weights included in the dataset and compute parameter estimates separately for each of the 10 plausible values, then aggregate them following PISA procedures. In the random forest (ML) step, they explicitly did not use replicate weights because random forests do not generate parameter estimates; thus, the ML variable-selection stage is not described as weight-aware.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Philippine PISA 2018 dataset for 15-year-old students (N=7233) selected via complex two-stage sampling. Excluded predictor variables with 100% missing information and removed redundant PISA index variables used to construct other indices (e.g., occupational status index used to derive ESCS). Removed variables that did not show statistically significant correlation with reading achievement in preliminary analyses, reducing the predictor set to 53 variables; then applied an 80% missingness threshold per case for missing-value analysis and retained all 7223 observations because each case had <25% missingness. Applied multiple imputation (MICE) for missing predictor/outcome data.

Learning time in language of test

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (Model 1): R²=0.66, RMSE=47.19; Random Forest (Model 2, top 26 predictors): R²=0.64, RMSE=47.50 (aggregated across 10 plausible values). HLM (using the 26 RF predictors): R²=0.53; effect sizes small-to-moderate; grade repetition largest by effect size in HLM.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (Philippines, 15-year-olds) the study leveraged self-concept of reading difficulty, socioeconomic status, grade repetition, school belongingness, and fixed mindset to predict reading achievement (PVREAD1–PVREAD10), finding that these variables were among the most important predictors and that self-concept of reading difficulty showed the highest impact in the RF model. This indicates that Philippine reading interventions may need to combine socioeconomic/school-environment supports with proximal learning experiences that build positive reading self-beliefs and metacognitive engagement, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Reading achievement for the Philippines (N=7233 15-year-olds) and predicts reading achievement using a two-step approach: Random Forest variable importance with cross-validation, followed by hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) for interpretable parameter estimates. For the Random Forest, the full model explained about 64–66% of variance in the unobserved sample (Model 1: R²=0.66, RMSE=47.19), while the streamlined model using the top 26 predictors achieved nearly the same performance (Model 2: R²=0.64, RMSE=47.50). The HLM using the same 26 predictors explained less variance (R²=0.53) and showed small-to-moderate effects, with grade repetition ranking highest by effect size. Key predictors included reading difficulty self-concept, socioeconomic status, grade repetition, school belonging, and fixed mindset, alongside proximal processes such as online reading time and summarizing metacognition. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causality) and the fact that the ML step does not use replicate weights, so population-representative uncertainty is handled primarily in the HLM stage.
